title: Operators in C
content:
Operators in C

C operators are symbols that are used to perform Sone specific operations on operands.

There are following types of operators in C.

 

  1. Arithmetic Operators
  2. Comparison (Relational) Operator
  3. Logical Operators
  4. Assignment Operators
  5. Bitwise Operators

1.Arithmetic Operators

Arithmetic operators are used to perform arithmetic operations on the operands. The following operators are known as C arithmetic operators.

 

Operator

Description

Example

+

Addition

10+20 = 30

-

Subtraction

20-10 = 10

*

Multiplication

10*20 = 200

/

Division

20/10 = 2

%

Modulus (Remainder)

20%10 = 0

++

Increment

Int a=10; a++; Now a = 11

 --

Decrement

Int a=10; a--; Now a = 9 

2.Comparison  Operators

The C comparison operator compares the two operands. The comparison operators are as follows:

Operator

Description

Example

==

Is equal to

10==20 = false

!=

Not equal to

10!=20 = true

>

Greater than

20>10 = true

>=

Greater than or equal to

20>=10 = true

<

Less than

20<10 = false

<=

Less than or equal to

20<=10 = false

3.Logical Operators

The following operators are known as C logical operators.

Operator

Description

Example

&&

Logical AND ( It returns true when both expression are true)

(10==20 && 20==33) = false

||

Logical OR( It returns true when one of both equations is true)

(10==20 || 20==20) = true

!

Logical Not (It return true when expression give false)

!(10==20) = true

4.Assignment Operators

The following operators are known as C assignment operators.

Operator

Description

Example

=

Assign

var a=6;

+=

Add and assign

int a=10; a+=20; Now a = 30

-=

Subtract and assign

int a=20; a-=10; Now a = 10

*=

Multiply and assign

int a=10; a*=20; Now a = 200

/=

Divide and assign

int a=10; a/=2; Now a = 5

%=

Modulus and assign

int a=10; a%=2; Now a = 0

5.Bitwise Operators

The bitwise operators perform bitwise operations on operands. The bitwise operators are as follows:

Operator

Description

Example

&

Bitwise AND

5 & 1  = 1

5 & 4  =  4

|

Bitwise OR

5 | 1 = 5

5 | 4 = 5

^

Bitwise XOR

5  ^ 1 = 4

5 ^ 4 = 1

~

Bitwise NOT

(~10) = -11

<<

Bitwise Left Shift

(10<<2) = 40

>>

Bitwise Right Shift

(10>>2) = 2

 

Note –

  • Formula for left shift – number * 2n
  • Formula for Right shift – number / 2n

title: Conditional Statements in C
content:
Conditional Statements

Conditional statements are used to perform different actions based on different conditions. Very often when you write code, you want to perform different actions for different decisions.

In C programming we have the following conditional statements:

  1. If statement
  2. If else statement
  3. If else if statement
  4. Nested If statement
  • Use if to specify a block of code to be executed, if a specified condition is true
  • Use else to specify a block of code to be executed, if the same condition is false
  • Use else if to specify a new condition to test, if the first condition is false

The if Statement

Use the if statement to specify a block of C code to be executed if a condition is true.

Syntax

if (condition) {

// block of code to be executed if the condition is true

}

Example: -

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int marks = 75;

    if (marks >= 50) {
        printf("You passed the exam!");
    }
    
    return 0;
}

Output: You passed the exam!

The else Statement

Use the else statement to specify a block of code to be executed if the condition is false.

Syntax -

if (condition) {

// block of code to be executed if the condition is true

}

else {

// block of code to be executed if the condition is false

}

Example :-

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int age = 16;

    if (age >= 18) {
        printf("Eligible to vote.");
    } else {
        printf("Not eligible to vote.");
    }
    
    return 0;
}

 Output: Not eligible to vote.

The else if Statement

Use the else if statement to specify a new condition if the first condition is false.

Syntax

if (condition1) {

// block of code to be executed if condition1 is true

}

else if (condition2) {

// block of code to be executed if the condition1 is false and condition2 is true

}

else {

// block of code to be executed if the condition1 is false and condition2 is false

}

Example:-

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int marks = 72;

    if (marks >= 90) {
        printf("Grade: A\n");
    } else if (marks >= 75) {
        printf("Grade: B\n");
    } else if (marks >= 60) {
        printf("Grade: C\n");
    } else {
        printf("Grade: F\n");
    }
    
    return 0;
}

Output: Grade: C

title: Loop
content:
Loops in C 

  • A loop is a control structure that allows you to execute a block of code repeatedly based on a condition.
  • Loops are essential for automating repetitive tasks and keeping your code DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

1. Core Components of a Loop

  • Initialization: Setting a starting value for the loop counter variable.
  • Condition: A boolean expression that determines if the loop should continue running.
  • Update (Increment/Decrement): Modifying the loop counter variable after each iteration so the condition eventually becomes false.

2. Types of Loops in C

C provides three primary types of loops. They are categorized into two groups:

  • Entry-controlled loops: The condition is checked before entering the loop body (for, while).
  • Exit-controlled loops: The condition is checked after executing the loop body at least once (do...while).

A. The while Loop

Best used when you do not know the exact number of iterations beforehand, and the loop depends purely on a condition remaining true.

initialization;
while (condition) {
    // Code to be executed
    update;
}

Example:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int count = 1; // Initialization
    while (count <= 5) { // Condition
        printf("%d ", count);
        count++; // Update
    }
    return 0;
}

B. The for Loop

Best used when you know exactly how many times you want the loop to run. All three loop components are written on a single line, making it compact.

for (initialization; condition; update) {
    // Code to be executed
}

Example:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    // Prints numbers 1 to 5
    for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
        printf("%d ", i);
    }
    return 0;
}

C. The do...while Loop

Unlike the other loops, a do...while loop guarantees that the code block will execute at least once, even if the condition is false from the start.

initialization;
do {
    // Code to be executed
    update;
} while (condition); // Note the semicolon here!

Example:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int i = 10;
    do {
        printf("%d ", i); // This will print "10" even though 10 is not < 5
        i++;
    } while (i < 5);
    return 0;
}

title: Dictionary part 2
content:
10. Dictionary Comprehension

Dictionary comprehension provides a concise way to create dictionaries from iterables or other dictionaries.

Syntax:

new_dict = {key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable if condition}

 

Examples:

# Squares of numbers 1 to 5

squares = {x: x**2 for x in range(1, 6)}

print(squares)   # {1:1, 2:4, 3:9, 4:16, 5:25}

 

# Filter: only even squares

even_sq = {x: x**2 for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0}

print(even_sq)   # {2:4, 4:16, 6:36, 8:64, 10:100}

 

# Swap keys and values

original = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}

swapped  = {v: k for k, v in original.items()}

print(swapped)   # {1:'a', 2:'b', 3:'c'}

 

# Convert two lists into a dictionary

keys   = ['name', 'age', 'city']

values = ['Alice', 21, 'Delhi']

d = {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}

print(d)   # {'name':'Alice', 'age':21, 'city':'Delhi'}

 

11. Nested Dictionaries

A dictionary can contain another dictionary as a value, creating a nested structure. This is useful for representing complex, hierarchical data.

students = {

    'Alice': {'age': 21, 'marks': 95, 'grade': 'A'},

    'Bob'  : {'age': 22, 'marks': 88, 'grade': 'B'},

    'Carol': {'age': 20, 'marks': 73, 'grade': 'C'}

}

 

# Accessing nested values

print(students['Alice']['marks'])   # 95

print(students['Bob']['grade'])     # B

 

# Adding a new student

students['Dave'] = {'age': 23, 'marks': 80, 'grade': 'B'}

 

# Iterating over nested dictionary

for name, info in students.items():

    print(name, '->', info['marks'])

 

 

 

 

12. Linear Search in Dictionary

12.1 Search by Key

student = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 21, 'grade': 'A'}

search_key = 'age'

found = False

 

for key in student:

    if key == search_key:

        found = True

        print('Key found! Value:', student[key])

        break

 

if not found:

    print('Key not found')

 

# Output: Key found! Value: 21

 

12.2 Search by Value

student = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 21, 'grade': 'A'}

search_val = 21

found = False

 

for key, value in student.items():

    if value == search_val:

        found = True

        print('Value found! Key:', key)

        break

 

if not found:

    print('Value not found')

 

# Output: Value found! Key: age

 

13. Counting Frequency Using a Dictionary

Dictionaries are excellent for counting how many times each element appears in a sequence.

# Count frequency of characters in a string

text = 'hello world'

freq = {}

 

for ch in text:

    if ch in freq:

        freq[ch] += 1

    else:

        freq[ch]  = 1

 

print(freq)

# {'h':1, 'e':1, 'l':3, 'o':2, ' ':1, 'w':1, 'r':1, 'd':1}

 

# Shorter version using get()

freq2 = {}

for ch in text:

    freq2[ch] = freq2.get(ch, 0) + 1

 

# Count word frequencies in a sentence  ( we discuss about this after learning string functions)

sentence = 'apple banana apple cherry banana apple'

words     = sentence.split()

word_freq = {}

for word in words:

    word_freq[word] = word_freq.get(word, 0) + 1

print(word_freq)   # {'apple':3, 'banana':2, 'cherry':1}

 

14. Merging Dictionaries

d1 = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}

d2 = {'c': 3, 'd': 4}

 

d1.update(d2)

print(d1)   # {'a':1, 'b':2, 'c':3, 'd':4}

 

 

15. Dictionary vs List vs Tuple

Feature

Dictionary

List

Tuple

Syntax

{ key: value }

[ ]

( )

Ordered

Yes (3.7+)

Yes

Yes

Mutable

Yes

Yes

No

Indexed by

Key (any immutable)

Integer

Integer

Duplicates

Keys: No, Values: Yes

Yes

Yes

Use Case

Key-value mapping

Ordered items

Fixed data

Speed (lookup)

O(1) avg.

O(n)

O(n)

 

16. Common Errors with Dictionaries

Error

Cause

Example

KeyError

Accessing a key that does not exist

d['city'] when 'city' not in d

TypeError

Using a mutable type (list) as a key

d[[1,2]] = 'val'

AttributeError

Calling a wrong method name

d.append('x')  (no append in dict)

TypeError

Iterating with wrong assumption

for i in range(len(d)): d[i]

 

17. Practical Programs

17.1 Student Report Card

report = {}
n = int(input("Number of students: "))
for _ in range(n):
    name  = input("Name: ")
    marks = float(input("Marks: "))
    report[name] = marks
print("\n--- Report Card ---")
for name, marks in report.items():
    if marks >= 90:
        grade = "A"
    elif marks >= 75:
        grade = "B"
    else:
        grade = "C"
    print(f"{name}: {marks} -> Grade {grade}")
topper = max(report, key=report.get)
print(f"Topper: {topper} with {report[topper]} marks")

 

17.2 Phone Book Application

phonebook = {}

while True:
    print("\n--- Phonebook Menu ---")
    print("1. Add Contact")
    print("2. Search Contact")
    print("3. Delete Contact")
    print("4. Show All Contacts")
    print("5. Exit")
    choice = input("Enter choice (1-5): ")
    if choice == "1":
        name = input("Enter name: ")
        number = input("Enter number: ")
        phonebook[name] = number
        print(f"{name} added.")
    elif choice == "2":
        name = input("Enter name to search: ")
        if name in phonebook:
            print(f"{name}: {phonebook[name]}")
        else:
            print("Contact not found.")
    elif choice == "3":
        name = input("Enter name to delete: ")
        if name in phonebook:
            del phonebook[name]
            print(f"{name} deleted.")
        else:
            print("Contact not found.")
    elif choice == "4":
        print("\n--- All Contacts ---")
        for name, number in phonebook.items():
            print(f"{name}: {number}")
    elif choice == "5":
        print("Exiting Phonebook. Goodbye!")
        break
    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Try again.")

title: Introduction to Arduino
content:
Introduction to Arduino

 

Arduino was a project started at Interaction Design Institute Ivrea (IDII) in Ivrea, Italy, with its primary goal being creating affordable and straightforward tools for non-engineers to use and create digital projects.

  • It is an open-source platform used for building electronics projects.
  • It consists of both a physical programmable circuit board and software (IDE) that runs on your computer, used to write and upload code to the board
  • Embedded C programming plays a key role in making the microcontroller perform desired actions.
  • Everyday devices like mobile phones, washing machines, security systems, and refrigerators are controlled by embedded programs.

Arduino consists of two main components: the Hardware (Arduino Board) and the software. (Arduino IDE) 

We will begin by studying the hardware, which includes different types of Arduino boards, and afterwards we will explore the software, known as the Arduino IDE

 

Arduino UNO R3 — Hardware Overview

The Arduino UNO is based on the ATmega328P microcontroller and is the most widely used Arduino board. It is ideal for beginners and makers.

 

2.1 Key Specifications

Feature

Specification

Microcontroller

ATmega328P

Operating Voltage

5V

Input Voltage

7-12V (recommended)

Digital I/O Pins

14 (6 PWM outputs)

Analog Input Pins

6 (A0-A5)

Flash Memory

32 KB (0.5 KB bootloader)

SRAM

2 KB

EEPROM

1 KB

Clock Speed

16 MHz

USB Connection

USB Type-B

 

2.2 Major Components

1. USB Plug/Connector

A printer USB port (USB Type-B) used to upload programs from the Arduino IDE. It also powers the board at 500mA, 5V from a Laptop/PC.

2. Power Supply / External Power

The barrel connector (2.1mm center-positive) accepts an AC-to-DC adapter or battery. The UNO operates at 5V but supports up to 20V input. Recommended input: 6-12V.

 

3. Voltage Regulator

Converts external input voltage to a regulated 5V supply for the board components.

 

4. ATmega328P Microcontroller

The brain of the Arduino UNO. It runs the uploaded program, controls I/O pins, and manages communication.

 

5. Crystal Oscillator (16 MHz)

Provides the clock signal for the microcontroller, determining how fast instructions are executed.

 

6. Reset Button

Restarts the currently loaded program. Useful for re-running a sketch without re-uploading.

 

7. ICSP Header

In-Circuit Serial Programming header, used to program the microcontroller directly, bypassing the bootloader.

 

2.3 Input/Output (I/O) Pins

Power Pins

  • GND — Ground pins (3 available to ground the circuit)
  • 5V — Provides regulated 5V output to components
  • 3.3V — Provides regulated 3.3V output
  • VIN — Input voltage to board when using external power
  • AREF — Analog reference voltage for ADC
  • IOREF — Reference for shields to adapt to the board's voltage

 

Analog Input Pins (A0-A5)

These 6 pins read analog signals (0-5V) and convert them to digital values (0-1023) using a 10-bit ADC.

Used with sensors like temperature, light, or pressure sensors.

 

Digital Pins (0-13)

These pins can be used as either INPUT or OUTPUT. When used as OUTPUT, they provide 5V (HIGH) or 0V (LOW).

When used as INPUT, they read external signals.

 

PWM Pins (~) — Pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11

Marked with a tilde (~). These digital pins can simulate analog output using Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) with 8-bit resolution (0-255) via the analogWrite() function

 

 Some Other Types of Arduino Boards

  • Arduino Uno (R3) — Most popular, beginner-friendly
  • Arduino Nano — Compact version of Uno
  • Arduino Micro — Even smaller, USB HID capable
  • Arduino Due — 32-bit ARM processor, 84 MHz
  • Arduino Mega (R3) — 54 digital I/O pins, for large projects
  • Arduino Leonardo — Built-in USB communication
  • LilyPad Arduino — Wearable electronics
  • Arduino Bluetooth — Built-in Bluetooth
  • Arduino Ethernet — Built-in Ethernet
  • Arduino Zero — 32-bit SAMD21 microcontroller

Note - In our Syllabus we only Study about Arduino Uno Board.

title: Arduino IDE
content:
Arduino IDE

Arduino IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is the open-source software Arduino.

It is a text editor like a notepad with different features.

It is used for writing code, compiling the code to check if any errors are there, and uploading the code to the Arduino.

It is a cross-platform software which is available for every Operating System like Windows, Linux, macOS. It supports C/C++ language.

Installing Arduino IDE

  1. Go to https://www.arduino.cc/en/software
  2. Download the appropriate version for your OS (Windows/Mac/Linux)
  3. Install the software with default settings
  4. Connect Arduino board via USB cable
  5. Go to Tools > Board > Select 'Arduino Uno'
  6. Go to Tools > Port > Select the COM port

IDE Interface 

 

Structure of an Arduino Sketch

Every Arduino sketch has two mandatory functions:

 

void setup() {

  // Runs ONCE when the board powers up or resets

  // Initialize pin modes, serial communication, etc.

}

 

void loop() {

  // Runs REPEATEDLY forever

  // Main program logic goes here

}

 

Note: Both setup() and loop() must always be present even if empty.

title: Functions
content:
Python Functions

 

1. Introduction to Functions

A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task. Functions help break down complex programs into smaller, manageable parts, improving readability and efficiency.

                                                                                                                     OR

In Python, a function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task. You define a function once, and then you can call (use) it anywhere in your code.

                                                                              OR

A function is a block of code which only runs when it is called. You can pass data, known as parameters, into a function. A function can return data as a result. 

 

Key points about functions:

  • A function is defined once and can be called multiple times
  • Functions help divide a large program into smaller, manageable sub-problems
  • They make code more readable, reusable, and easier to debug
  • Python has built-in functions like print(), len(), etc., and also allows creating user-defined functions

 

2. Advantages of Using Functions

1.  Program development made easy and fast – Work can be divided among project members, so implementation can be completed faster.

2.  Program testing becomes easy – Easy to locate and isolate a faulty function for further investigation.

3.  Code sharing becomes possible – A function written once may be reused by many other programs; a programmer can use functions written by others instead of starting from scratch.

4.  Code re-usability increases – A function avoids rewriting the same block of code that is needed in two or more places in a program, especially when the code is long or complicated.

5.  Increases program readability – The length of the source program can be reduced by calling functions at appropriate places, making the program more readable.

6.  Function facilitates procedural abstraction – Once a function is written, the programmer only needs to know how to invoke it, not how it is coded internally.

7.  Functions facilitate the factoring of code – A function can be called inside another function, enabling code decomposition.

 

3. Types of Functions in Python

Type

Description

Examples

Built-in Functions

Pre-defined functions, always available without importing anything.

print(), len(), type(), int(), input(), range(), abs(), max(), min()

Functions in Modules

Predefined in specific modules; can only be used after importing the module.

math.sqrt(), math.ceil(), random.randint(), os.getcwd()

User-defined Functions

Created by the programmer to perform a specific task as needed by the program.

def greet(): ...   def calcSum(x,y): ...

Lambda Functions

Small anonymous functions defined using the lambda keyword for single expressions.

lambda x: x * 2   lambda a,b: a+b

3.1.Built In Functions

These functions are already built in the python library.

  • These are pre-defined functions and are always available for use
  • In order to use these functions , there is no need to import any module
  • We can directly use it , in our program.

                            Example: len()   ,  print()   ,  int()   , input()   , type()  , id() ,ord()

title: Arduino Functions
content:
Arduino Functions

There are following types of function in arduino -

1. Main Structure Functions — setup() & loop()

2. Digital I/O Functions

3. Analog I/O Functions

4. Time Functions

5. Math & Mapping Functions

6. Serial Communication Functions

 

1. Main Structure Functions

Every Arduino sketch must contain these two functions. setup() runs once on power-on or reset; loop() repeats continuously.

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

setup()

void setup() { ... }

No parameter.
Runs once at start.
Returns void.

void setup(){
   Serial.begin(9600);
pinMode(13, OUTPUT);
}

loop()

void loop() { ... }

No parameter.
Runs repeatedly forever.
Returns void.
Main Code here

void loop(){
digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
delay(1000);
}

 

 

2. Digital I/O Functions

Used to read from and write to digital pins. Pins operate at 0V (LOW) or 5V (HIGH).

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

pinMode()

pinMode(pin, mode)

pin: int (pin number)
mode: INPUT, OUTPUT
 Returns: void

pinMode(13, OUTPUT); pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);

digitalWrite()

digitalWrite(pin, value)

pin: int (pin number)
value: HIGH (1) or LOW (0)
Returns: void

digitalWrite(13, HIGH); digitalWrite(13, LOW);

digitalRead()

int digitalRead(pin)

pin: int(pin number)
Returns: HIGH (1) or LOW (0)

int val = digitalRead(2);

 

 

3. Analog I/O Functions

Read analog voltages (ADC, 10-bit) and output PWM signals. analogWrite() requires a PWM-capable pin (~).

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

analogRead()

int analogRead(pin)

pin: A0–A5 (analog pin)
Returns: int 0–1023 (10-bit ADC)

int sensorVal = analogRead(A0); float voltage = sensorVal*(5.0/1023.0);

analogWrite()

analogWrite(pin, value)

pin: PWM-capable pin (~)
value: 0–255 (duty cycle)
Returns: void

analogWrite(9, 128);

 

 

4. Time Functions

Control timing and measure elapsed time. Prefer millis()/micros() over delay() in non-blocking designs.

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

delay()

delay(ms)

ms: unsigned long (milliseconds) Pauses program execution Returns: void

delay(1000); // Pause for 1 second

delayMicroseconds()

delayMicroseconds(us)

us: unsigned int (microseconds) Pauses for very short times Returns: void

delayMicroseconds(100); // Pause for 100 µs

millis()

unsigned long millis()

No params Returns: unsigned long — ms since program started. Overflows ~49.7 days.

unsigned long t = millis(); if (millis() - t > 1000) { ... }

micros()

unsigned long micros()

No params Returns: unsigned long — µs since program started. Overflows ~70 min.

unsigned long start = micros(); // measure pulse width

 

 

5. Math & Mapping Functions

Utility math functions built into Arduino. map() is especially useful for scaling sensor readings to output ranges.

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

map()

long map(value, fromLow, fromHigh, toLow, toHigh)

value: input number fromLow/High: input range toLow/High: output range Returns: long (mapped value)

int out = map(analogRead(A0), 0,1023,0, 255);
analogWrite(9, out);

abs()

abs(x)

x: int or float Returns: absolute value of x

int diff = abs(a - b); // always positive

min() / max()

min(a, b) max(a, b)

a, b: any numeric type Returns: smaller / larger of the two values

int lo = min(x, y);
int hi = max(x, y);

sq() / sqrt()

sq(x) sqrt(x)

x: numeric sq returns x² sqrt returns square root (double)

double h = sqrt(sq(3) + sq(4)); // h = 5.0

 

 

6. Serial Communication Functions

Communicate with a computer or other devices via USB/UART. Always call Serial.begin() in setup() before using Serial functions.

Function

Syntax

Parameters / Returns

Example

Serial.begin()

Serial.begin(speed)

speed: long baud rate (e.g. 9600, 115200)
Returns: void

void setup(){
Serial.begin(9600);}

Serial.print()

Serial.print(val) Serial.print(val, format)

val: any type
format: BIN, OCT, DEC, HEX, or decimal places Returns: bytes written

Serial.print("Temp: "); Serial.print(temp, 2); Serial.print(255, HEX);

Serial.println()

Serial.println(val)

Same as print() but appends \r\n
Returns: bytes written

Serial.println("Hello!"); Serial.println(analogRead(A0));

Serial.read()

int Serial.read()

No params Returns: first byte of incoming data, or -1 if none

if (Serial.available()) {   char c = Serial.read(); }

Serial.available()

int Serial.available()

No params Returns: number of bytes in receive buffer (0 if empty)

while (Serial.available() > 0) {   char c = Serial.read(); }

Serial.end()

Serial.end()

No params. Disables serial communication. Returns: void

Serial.end(); // frees pins 0 & 1

2. Functions in Module

 1. What is a Module?

A module is a file containing Python definitions (functions, classes, variables) that can be imported and reused in other programs. Python ships with a rich standard library of built-in modules, and you can also install third-party modules via pip.

Key benefits:

  •  Code reusability — write once, use anywhere

  •  Organisation — split large programs into logical files

  •  Namespace management — avoids name conflicts

  •  Access to Python's standard library (~200+ built-in modules)

 

2.  Ways to Import a Module

Meaning

Example usage

import module

from math import sqrt
sqrt(9)

from module import *

from math import *
sqrt(9)

import module as alias

Give module a short alias

m.sqrt(9)
