title: What is Scope? & LEGB
content:
What is Scope ?

In Python, scope refers to the region of a program where a particular variable (name) is accessible. Python uses a namespace to manage these variables.

Key Terms

Term

Meaning

Name

A variable identifier (e.g., x, total, my_func)

Object

The actual data the name refers to (e.g., 42, 'Hello', [1,2,3])

Scope

The region where a name is visible and accessible

Namespace

A dictionary-like mapping of names to objects

Binding

Assigning a name to an object using the = operator

 

Types of Scope

  • Local Scope: Variables defined inside a function. Accessible only within that function.
  • Enclosing Scope: Variables in the outer function when functions are nested.
  • Global Scope: Variables defined at the top level of a module/script.
  • Built-in Scope: Python pre-defined names like print(), len(), range(), etc.

Example

x = 10           # Global scope

 

def my_func():

    y = 20       # Local scope

    print(x)     # Accesses global x  ->  10

    print(y)     # Accesses local y   ->  20

 

my_func()

# print(y)      # NameError! y is local to my_func

 

Note: A name assigned inside a function is local to that function by default, even if a global variable with the same name exists.

The LEGB Rule 

The LEGB Rule is the name resolution order Python follows when looking up a variable.

Python searches scopes in the fixed order L -> E -> G -> B. It stops at the first match.

If not found anywhere, a NameError is raised.

 

Letter

Full Name

Where Defined

Example

L

Local

Inside current function

x = 1 inside def f()

E

Enclosing

Outer function (nested)

x in outer() accessed by inner()

G

Global

Module top level

x = 10 outside all functions

B

Built-in

Python interpreter

print(), len(), range()

 

L — Local Scope

def greet():

    name = 'Alice'    # Local variable

    print(name)       # Found in Local  ->  Alice

 

E — Enclosing Scope (Nested Functions)

def outer():

    msg = 'Hello'        # Enclosing variable

    def inner():

        print(msg)       # Found in Enclosing  ->  Hello

    inner()

outer()

 

G — Global Scope

total = 100           # Global variable

def show():

    print(total)       # Found in Global  ->  100

 

B — Built-in Scope

print(len('Python'))  # len() is from Built-in scope  ->  6

 

The global Keyword

To modify a global variable inside a function, use the global keyword. Without it, Python creates a new local variable instead.

 

count = 0

def increment():

    global count        # Declare intent to use global

    count += 1

increment()

increment()

print(count)           # 2

 

Note: Without 'global count', the statement count += 1 causes UnboundLocalError because Python treats count as an uninitialized local variable.

The nonlocal Keyword

Used in nested functions to modify a variable from the enclosing (outer) function's scope.

 

def outer():

    x = 10

    def inner():

        nonlocal x      # Refers to outer's x, not global

        x += 5

    inner()

    print(x)            # 15

outer()

title: What is Moudule ?
content:
What is Module?

A module is a .py file containing Python definitions and statements (functions, classes, variables). Modules allow you to organize and reuse code across multiple programs.

  • File Extension: Every Python module is a .py file
  • Purpose: Code reuse, organization, namespace separation
  • Built-in Modules: math, os, sys, random, datetime, json, etc.
  • Custom Modules: Any .py file you create yourself

 

Why Use Modules?

  • Avoid repeating code across multiple programs
  • Organize large programs into manageable separate files
  • Share code between different projects
  • Use Python's rich standard library of ready-made tools
  • Prevent name conflicts using separate namespaces

 

Importing a Module — import Statement

import math

print(math.pi)           # 3.141592653589793

print(math.sqrt(16))     # 4.0

print(math.factorial(5)) # 120

 

Note: After 'import math', all names must be accessed with dot notation: math.function_name()

from...import Statement

from math import pi, sqrt

print(pi)         # 3.141592...  (no need to write math.pi)

print(sqrt(25))   # 5.0

 

Importing with Alias — as keyword

import numpy as np            # Common alias in data science

from math import factorial as fact

print(fact(6))    # 720

 

from...import * (Import Everything)

from math import *

print(sin(0))     # 0.0

print(cos(0))     # 1.0

 

Note: 'from module import *' is discouraged in large programs as it pollutes the namespace and makes it hard to trace where names come from.

 

Import Styles — Comparison

Import Style

Syntax

Access Style

Use Case

Full module

import math

math.sqrt()

Avoid name conflicts

Specific names

from math import sqrt

sqrt()

Frequently used functions

With alias

import math as m

m.sqrt()

Shorten long module names

All names

from math import *

sqrt()

Quick scripts only

 

What is Namespace?

A namespace is a container that holds a collection of names and their associated objects. Every module has its own namespace — names in one module do NOT clash with names in another module.

 

How Modules Create Namespaces

When you import a module, Python executes the module file and creates a module namespace.

All names defined in that file become attributes of the module object.

 

# mymodule.py

x = 100

def greet():

    print('Hello from mymodule!')

 

# main.py

import mymodule

print(mymodule.x)        # 100

mymodule.greet()         # Hello from mymodule!

 

Note: mymodule.x accesses name x inside mymodule's namespace — no collision even if you also have a variable named x in your own program.

title: Reloading Module
content:
Reloding Modules 

 

Why Reload a Module?

Since Python caches modules in sys.modules, if you change a module's source code after importing it, re-running import will NOT pick up the changes.

To force Python to re-read the updated file, use importlib.reload()

 

Syntax

from importlib import reload

reload(module_name)

 

Step-by-Step Example

import mymodule              # First import -- loaded and cached

 

# (You edit mymodule.py now...)

 

import mymodule              # Re-import -- uses cache, NO changes!

 

from importlib import reload

reload(mymodule)             # Reload -- re-reads file, picks up changes!

 

Practical Example — Config File

# config.py  ->  DEBUG = False

import config

print(config.DEBUG)          # False

 

# (You update config.py: DEBUG = True)

 

import config                # Re-import does nothing

print(config.DEBUG)          # Still False! (cached)

 

from importlib import reload

reload(config)

print(config.DEBUG)          # True  (reloaded from disk)

 

When is reload() Useful?

  • Interactive development in Python shell or Jupyter Notebook
  • When a module file changes during program execution
  • Testing and debugging without restarting the interpreter
  • Live configuration files that update dynamically

 

Important Points About reload()

Point

Explanation

Must import first

Module must already be imported before reloading

Partial update risk

Objects created from old version still use old code

Not recursive

Module dependencies are NOT automatically reloaded

sys.modules updated

Entry in sys.modules is refreshed after reload

Python 3 only syntax

from importlib import reload (not built-in in Python 3)

 

import vs reload — Key Difference

import (repeated)

reload(module)

Uses cached version from sys.modules

Re-executes the module file from disk

Does NOT pick up file changes

DOES pick up file changes

Fast (no file I/O)

Slower (reads and compiles the file again)

Default Python behavior

Requires explicit importlib.reload() call

title: Dimensions of Array
content:
Array Dimensions

A dimension in NumPy is one level of array depth.

Arrays inside arrays are called nested arrays.

 

Types of Arrays

0-D Array (Scalar)

A single value — the most basic element in NumPy.

import numpy as np

arr = np.array(42)

print(arr)          # 42

print(arr.ndim)     # 0

 

1-D Array (Unidimensional)

1D array Contains 0-D array as Elements .

Most common type.

arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

print(arr.ndim)     # 1

 

2-D Array (Matrix )

2D array Has 1-D arrays as its elements. Used for matrices.

NumPy provides numpy.mat sub-module for matrix operations.

arr = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

print(arr.ndim)     # 2

 

3-D Array (3rd Order Tensor)

Has 2-D arrays as its elements.

arr = np.array([[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]])

print(arr.ndim)     # 3

 

Higher-Dimensional Arrays

Use the ndmin argument to set any number of dimensions at creation time.

arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4], ndmin=5)

print(arr.ndim)     # 5

Note: The ndim attribute returns an integer showing how many dimensions an array has.

Note : 0-D = scalar, 1-D = vector, 2-D = matrix, 3-D = tensor. Know this for MCQs.
